analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on the largest inherited estates from 40 percent to 20 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 15, 2018 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top tax rate on large inherited estates — and on very large gifts and transfers that skip a generation — from 40% to 20%. The estate tax only applies to fortunes above a large exemption (over $11 million per person at the time), so the cut would go almost entirely to a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year. The bill also exempts its own cost from pay-as-it-goes budget rules, meaning it would add to deficits without any offset. It was introduced late in the 115th Congress, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — those above the multi-million-dollar exemption — would pay roughly half as much tax on inherited wealth, and the families making the largest lifetime gifts would also benefit. Only a few thousand very wealthy families pay any estate tax at all in a given year, so the benefit would be concentrated at the top.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top rate on estates, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers from 40% to 20%, reducing the tax owed on transfers of very large fortunes.
Exempts the revenue loss from Pay-As-You-Go scorecards, so the tax cut would not automatically trigger offsets under budget law.
Applies to deaths, gifts, and transfers after December 31, 2018, making the cut immediate.

analysis.who_pays: The public generally: the bill does not offset the lost revenue, so the deficit grows unless other taxes rise or spending falls. It would also make it cheaper to build dynastic wealth that is passed to heirs untaxed.

drawbacks.text: The bill would cut the top rate on the largest estates, gifts, and dynasty transfers from 40% to 20%, with the benefit flowing almost entirely to families with multi-million-dollar estates and wealth passed across generations.

The bill exempts its own revenue loss from Pay-As-You-Go budget rules, meaning the roughly $100 billion-plus cost of halving the estate tax would add to deficits with no offset, or be paid for later through cuts to other programs or higher taxes on everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The only substantive effect is a large tax cut for multi-million-dollar estates, and it is not paid for: the bill explicitly exempts itself from the pay-as-you-go rules that require tax cuts to be offset [S2][S3]. The cost lands on the general fund, either as debt or as cuts elsewhere. The bill also made no progress — it never received even a committee hearing before the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl introduced the bill on November 15, 2018, in the final weeks of the 115th Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill expired with the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Estate-tax opponents came out ahead in the sense that no vote ever forced members on record, but no one gained or lost money since the bill never moved. Wealthy estates continue paying the current 40% top rate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died in committee

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 15, 2018 and it was referred to the Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and it never advanced to a vote where the split could be measured.

industries.industry: Very wealthy families and large estates
industries.note: The bill cuts the tax rate on transfers of large fortunes from 40% to 20%, roughly halving the bill on estates of decedents dying after 2018 [S2][S3].
A permanent lower rate on large transfers sustains demand for sophisticated estate and gift planning services [S3].
